story.headline: Ultrafast Light Pulses Track Molecular Motion with Three-Femtosecond Resolution
story.summary: Researchers have tracked the coordinated motion of electrons and nuclei immediately following light absorption with a temporal resolution of three femtoseconds. This breakthrough provides new insights into ultrafast molecular dynamics and photochemistry.

draft.body:
An international research team led by the Politecnico di Milano has developed an experimental apparatus capable of tracking the coordinated motion of electrons and nuclei during photochemical reactions with a temporal resolution of approximately 3 femtoseconds. Reported in an announcement by [Politecnico di Milano](https://www.polimi.it/en/press-room/press-releases/translate-to-english-dettaglio/tre-femtosecondi-per-osservare-una-molecola-mentre-cambia), the technique uses ultrafast light pulses to record intermediate molecular configurations in the very first instants after a molecule absorbs light. One femtosecond equals one millionth of one billionth of a second, giving the platform extreme temporal precision in observing rapid structural evolution.

The findings were published in [Nature Communications](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-76602-4) under the European Research Council (ERC) Synergy TOMATTO project. The study was carried out by researchers from the Department of Physics at Politecnico di Milano, the Institute for Photonics and Nanotechnologies of the National Research Council of Italy (CNR), Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh, and the University of Bologna.

## How Ultrafast Light Pulses Capture Molecular Transitions

The measurement system operates on a pump-probe architecture integrated into a specialized beamline that synchronizes two distinct light pulses with extreme precision. As outlined by [Politecnico di Milano](https://www.polimi.it/en/the-politecnico/news/news-detail/osservare-linvisibile-la-nuova-frontiera-della-chimica-ultrarapida), the first pulse sits in the ultraviolet (UV) range. When directed into a gas-phase target sample, this UV pulse is absorbed by the molecule, triggering electronic excitation and driving its initial physical transformation.

[[FIG1]]

The second pulse arrives after a precisely controlled time interval. Emitted in the extreme ultraviolet (XUV) spectrum and lasting only a few attoseconds, this probe pulse interrogates the molecular state at that specific moment to reconstruct its characteristics through time-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy. By repeating the measurement sequence across incrementally stepped delays, the researchers construct a frame-by-frame progression showing how energy redistributes and how electrons and atomic nuclei move in coordination.

"With this apparatus, we can follow a molecule in the very first instants after it absorbs light, with a level of detail that was not previously accessible," said Mauro Nisoli, physics professor at Politecnico di Milano and coordinator of the ERC Synergy TOMATTO project. "It is like vastly increasing the number of frames in a film: a seemingly single transformation finally reveals all its intermediate stages."

## Tracking Conical Intersections in Acetylacetone

To demonstrate the capabilities of the experimental platform, the research team investigated acetylacetone, a standard model molecule used to study ultrafast light-driven chemical changes. According to the research summary released on [EurekAlert](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1148871), the 3-femtosecond temporal resolution allowed researchers to distinguish two successive passages through a conical intersection.

[[FIG2]]

A conical intersection acts as a crucial junction where electronic states meet, steering the excited molecule along a specific chemical reaction pathway. Previously available experimental instruments lacked the temporal resolution necessary to separate these rapid transition points in time. With the newly developed beamline, the team directly tracked the redistribution of internal energy and reconstructed the initial transformation stages triggered by light absorption.

"What we observe is the moment when light sets the molecule in motion and reorganises its internal energy," explained Maurizio Reduzzi, Associate Professor at the Department of Physics of Politecnico di Milano. Reduzzi stated that observing these stages directly allows researchers to get closer to the core of photochemical processes, where chemical transformations take shape.

## Attochemistry and Broader Research Applications

The experimental setup features an ultraviolet excitation stage with adjustable wavelengths. According to the [Politecnico di Milano](https://www.polimi.it/en/press-room/press-releases/translate-to-english-dettaglio/tre-femtosecondi-per-osservare-una-molecola-mentre-cambia) release, the ability to alter the UV pulse wavelength makes the system suitable for examining a wide variety of molecular targets and distinct electronic states.

The consortium plans to apply the method to more complex systems beyond acetylacetone. Prospective targets include biologically relevant molecules, photoactive materials, and molecular processes involved in energy conversion. The researchers also noted that the platform creates new opportunities for attochemistry, an emerging field exploring the observation and eventual control of chemical transformations by acting on electronic motion before the slower movement of atomic nuclei begins.

## Project Collaboration and Publication Details

The experimental investigation, titled "3-fs-resolved UV/XUV photoelectron spectroscopy in the gas phase," was authored by M. Pini and colleagues and published in [Nature Communications](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-76602-4). Support for the multi-institution project was provided by the European Research Council under grant agreement for the ERC Synergy TOMATTO initiative.

faq.a: A femtosecond is one millionth of one billionth of a second.

faq.q: How does the two-pulse pump-probe system work?
faq.a: An ultraviolet (UV) pulse initiates the molecular evolution, followed by an extreme ultraviolet (XUV) pulse lasting a few attoseconds that probes the molecular state at adjustable delay intervals via photoelectron spectroscopy.

faq.q: Which molecule was analyzed in the demonstration?
faq.a: The researchers analyzed acetylacetone, using the platform's 3-femtosecond resolution to distinguish two successive passages through a conical intersection.

faq.q: Who conducted and supported the research?
faq.a: The study was led by Politecnico di Milano in collaboration with the CNR Institute for Photonics and Nanotechnologies, Heriot-Watt University, and the University of Bologna, with funding from the European Research Council's ERC Synergy TOMATTO project.
